common_name: Rock Candy Blue Penstemon (Compact Early-Flowering Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Rock Candy Blue is part of a dwarf, uniform seed series bred for a first-year-flowering habit well under half the height of older Penstemon barbatus selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, since good drainage is essential to avoid crown rot in this disease-prone genus. Rock Candy Blue bears tightly packed, bell-shaped lavender-blue flowers on dense, compact spikes held well above a tidy basal mound, a scale that suits containers, rock gardens, and the front of a border where taller penstemon selections would overwhelm the space. It flowers over an unusually long season from spring into fall and draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds throughout, tolerating heat and drought well once established. Avoid rich soil or heavy fertilizer, which produce weak, floppy growth in penstemon generally.

common_name: Bejeweled Dark Amethyst Penstemon (Southwest Native Bearded Penstemon)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Bejeweled Dark Amethyst is a Southwest-native Penstemon barbatus selection bred for a tidy, floriferous habit and strong garden performance.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, adding gravel or coarse sand in heavy clay, since this Southwest native strongly resents sitting wet over winter. Bejeweled Dark Amethyst produces slender, tubular dark reddish-purple flowers held on upright spikes above a compact clump of narrow green foliage from late spring through summer, a long bloom season that keeps hummingbirds and bees visiting steadily. It tolerates heat and drought with ease once established and works well in borders, mass plantings, and as a cut flower. Avoid overly rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens the life of this otherwise long-lived perennial.

common_name: Midnight Masquerade Penstemon (Purple-Foliage Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Midnight Masquerade pairs deep eggplant-purple foliage with lavender-purple, white-throated flowers on a tall, upright hybrid penstemon.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; this hybrid penstemon keeps its deep, near-black purple leaf color through the growing season, giving strong foliage interest even before the tall spikes of lavender-purple, white-throated flowers open in early summer. Its substantial height suits the middle or back of a sunny border, where it draws bees and hummingbirds over a long bloom period. The plant tolerates heat, drought, and light soil salinity once established, and benefits from cutting back spent flower spikes to tidy the clump and encourage rebloom.

common_name: Onyx and Pearls Penstemon (Dark-Foliage Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Onyx and Pearls combines near-black foliage with soft lavender, white-throated flowers on a tall, vigorous hybrid penstemon.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry to average, well-drained soil; Onyx and Pearls is named for the contrast between its near-black foliage and its soft lavender flowers with white interiors, a combination that gives the plant ornamental value even between bloom flushes. Tall spikes of tubular flowers open in early summer and draw bees and hummingbirds reliably over several weeks. It tolerates heat, drought, and some soil salinity once established, and works well massed in a border or cut for arrangements. Good drainage through winter is essential, as with other bearded penstemon hybrids.

common_name: Maestro Coral Agastache (Long-Blooming Coral Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Maestro Coral produces an unusually long, continuous flush of coral-pink flower spikes without deadheading.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; drainage is critical, since agastache crowns rot quickly in soggy winter soil. Maestro Coral sends up a profusion of coral-pink flower spikes over aromatic, anise-scented foliage continuously from spring through fall, with no deadheading needed to keep it blooming. The long flowering season and nectar-rich spikes draw hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies steadily, while the plant resists deer browsing and tolerates heat and drought well once established. In colder zones, treat it as a heat-loving annual or bring cuttings indoors over winter.

common_name: Arizona Sunset Agastache (Dwarf Bicolor Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Arizona Sunset is a dwarf agastache with silver-green foliage and pink-and-purple bicolor flower spikes, well suited to containers and rock gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this dwarf selection stays compact and tidy without the sprawl common in larger agastache cultivars. Arizona Sunset carries short, dense spikes of pink-and-purple bicolor flowers over narrow, silvery-green, aromatic foliage from spring through fall, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds despite its small stature. It tolerates heat and drought with ease once established and resists deer, making it a reliable choice for a sunny rock garden, container, or border edge. Sharp drainage through winter is the key to bringing it back the following spring.

common_name: Blue Bayou Agastache (Indigo-Blue Anise Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Blue Bayou is a patented hybrid (USPP 35,759) bred to carry a true indigo-blue flower color on the same hardy, vigorous plant as its predecessors.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage remains essential, since agastache crowns rot readily in wet winter soil. Blue Bayou bears dense spikes of indigo-blue flowers over fragrant, anise-scented foliage from midsummer into early fall, a deeper, truer blue than most older blue-flowered agastache selections. The fragrant flowers draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds in steady numbers, and the plant tolerates heat and drought well once established. Leave the spent flower spikes standing into winter for additional structure and seed for finches.

common_name: Summerlong Coral Agastache (Salmon-Pink Mexican Giant Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Summerlong Coral is a Mexican giant hyssop selection with salmon-pink flower spikes and a sturdy, upright, fragrant-foliaged habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; good drainage limits the crown rot that affects agastache in heavy, wet soils. Summerlong Coral forms an upright clump of fragrant, aromatic foliage topped with salmon-pink flower spikes from late spring through summer, attracting bees and hummingbirds over an extended season. It handles heat well and resists deer browsing, making it a dependable thriller for containers or a sunny mixed border. In zones below 7 it is best treated as a heat-loving annual or overwintered from cuttings.

common_name: Catwalk Queen Catmint (Large-Flowered Hybrid Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Catwalk Queen carries noticeably larger lavender-blue flowers on longer panicles than most catmint cultivars, on a sturdy, mounded plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average, low-to-moderate moisture soil in full sun. Catwalk Queen produces unusually large lavender-blue flowers held in long, dense panicles over thick, sturdy green foliage, creating a fuller-looking bloom than most catmint selections while staying low and tidy. Bees and other pollinators visit the fragrant flowers steadily from late spring through summer, and shearing the plant back lightly after the first flush encourages a strong rebloom. It resists deer and rabbits and tolerates heat and drought well once established.

common_name: Lemon Purrfection Catmint (Golden-Foliage Early-Blooming Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Lemon Purrfection pairs golden-chartreuse foliage with lavender-blue flowers and blooms earlier than most catmint cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; foliage color develops best with consistent sun, turning more chartreuse in shadier spots. Lemon Purrfection opens its lavender-blue flowers earlier in the season than most catmint selections, holding them above golden-yellow foliage that provides season-long color even between bloom flushes. The tidy, compact mound suits edging, containers, and the front of a border, and shearing lightly after the first bloom cycle encourages continued flowering. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and is rarely troubled by deer or rabbits.

common_name: Chartreuse on the Loose Catmint (Bright Gold-Foliage Groundcover Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Chartreuse on the Loose is a low, wide-spreading catmint grown primarily for its bright chartreuse-yellow foliage and continuous summer bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, giving it room to spread since the mound grows notably wider than it is tall. Chartreuse on the Loose produces lavender-blue flowers over vivid chartreuse-yellow foliage from summer into early fall, and unlike many catmint cultivars it keeps flowering without any deadheading. Its low, spreading habit makes it a useful bright-colored edging or groundcover plant, and the aromatic foliage releases its fragrance readily when brushed. It tolerates heat fluctuations well and resists deer and rabbits.

common_name: Prelude Blue Japanese Catmint (Tall Moisture-Tolerant Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to evenly moist, average soil in full sun; Prelude Blue is a tall selection of Japanese catmint that tolerates more moisture and part shade than most Nepeta x faassenii cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike the drought-adapted Nepeta x faassenii hybrids, Nepeta subsessilis selections such as Prelude Blue tolerate regular moisture and even light shade without declining. It bears blue-purple flowers on upright stems well above the attractive mint-scented foliage, blooming from late spring through summer and again after a midsummer cutback. The plant takes two or three seasons to reach its full mature size and divides easily once established. Bees and other pollinators visit the flowers readily, and the foliage stays attractive even after a hard pruning.

common_name: Color Spires Azure Snow Salvia (Compact Hardy Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Azure Snow is part of the Color Spires series of hardy salvia bred for compact, uniform habit and deep violet-blue and white bicolor flower spikes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Azure Snow forms a neat, mounded clump of aromatic green foliage topped with upright spikes of deep violet-blue and white bicolor flowers from late spring through summer, with deadheading or a light shearing after the first flush encouraging a strong rebloom. It is drought-tolerant once established though it flowers more heavily with average, consistent moisture, and it resists both deer and rabbit browsing. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the flower spikes steadily throughout the long bloom season, and the plant performs reliably across a wide range of climates.

common_name: Living Large Big Sky Salvia (Oversized Hardy Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Big Sky is part of the Living Large series, bred for a larger overall scale than the Color Spires series while keeping the same hardy, reliable performance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, giving it more room than compact hardy salvia cultivars since it grows noticeably larger in both height and spread. Big Sky forms a dense rosette of large green leaves and blooms later in the season than most hardy salvia, sending up substantial spikes of violet-blue flowers in early summer. Cutting the plant back after the first bloom flush promotes reblooming later in the season, and established plants tolerate heat and drought well while flowering more heavily with average moisture. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers steadily, and the plant resists deer and rabbit damage.

common_name: Living Large Dark Sky Salvia (Oversized Hardy Meadow Sage)

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, giving it more room than compact hardy salvia cultivars since it grows noticeably larger in both height and spread. common_name: Arctic Blaze Fuchsia Salvia (Continuous-Blooming Bedding Sage)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Arctic Blaze Fuchsia has sturdy, flexible branches and blooms continuously from planting until frost without deadheading.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; this vegetatively propagated salvia grows into a wide, mounded plant with sturdy, flexible stems that resist breaking in wind and rain. Arctic Blaze Fuchsia produces deep pink flowers continuously from planting through the first hard frost without any deadheading, making it a low-maintenance choice for borders, mass plantings, and large containers. It attracts hummingbirds reliably and resists deer browsing, performing well in both humid southern summers and cooler northern ones. In zones 9-11 it may persist as a short-lived perennial, but elsewhere it is grown as a warm-season annual.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: OutShine Orchid Salvia (Rounded Ball-Form Bedding Sage)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; OutShine Orchid forms a rounded, ball-shaped plant covered in small orchid-pink flowers from spring to frost.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; this vegetatively propagated hybrid grows into a dense, rounded mound rather than the taller, looser habit of older bedding salvias. OutShine Orchid produces a steady flush of small, bright orchid-pink flowers from spring through hard frost with minimal care, performing reliably in both cool northern seasons and hot, humid southern summers. It tolerates drought once established, resists deer browsing, and draws pollinators consistently over its long bloom season. In the warmest zones it may behave as a short-lived perennial.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: OutShine Red Salvia (Rounded Ball-Form Bedding Sage)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; OutShine Red (patented as Novasalred) forms a dense, rounded mound covered continuously in small cherry-red flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; like other OutShine selections, this patented cultivar holds a tidy, upright, mounded form rather than sprawling as the season progresses. OutShine Red bears cherry-red flowers continuously across its rounded habit from spring through hard frost, needing little more than occasional watering to keep performing in both cool and hot, humid climates. It tolerates drought once established and resists deer browsing while attracting pollinators steadily. Avoid overwatering, which can encourage root problems in this otherwise low-maintenance bedding salvia.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Unplugged Pink Salvia (Sterile Non-Stop-Blooming Bedding Sage)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Unplugged Pink is a sterile hybrid that produces no seed, so it blooms continuously without deadheading.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun after frost danger has passed; because this hybrid is sterile and sets no seed, it channels all of its energy into continuous flowering rather than seed production. Unplugged Pink bears pink-to-fuchsia flowers with a contrasting black calyx over deep green foliage from planting until frost, tolerating heat and humidity with ease. It responds well to a hard trim if it becomes leggy, quickly regrowing bushier and more floriferous, and it attracts hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies while resisting deer browsing. Regular watering keeps it looking its best, though it tolerates short dry spells once established.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Unplugged Red Scarlet Sage (Compact Non-Stop-Blooming Salvia coccinea)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun; Unplugged Red is a compact, patented Salvia coccinea selection (a mutation of 'Forest Fire') that blooms non-stop through heat and humidity.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun after frost danger has passed; this compact scarlet sage selection stays mid-sized rather than growing as tall and open as the wild species. Unplugged Red produces scarlet-red tubular flowers on mid-sized plants that bloom for months in heat and humidity with minimal deadheading required. It attracts hummingbirds and other pollinators reliably, tolerates drought once established, and resists deer browsing. Regular watering and feeding keep it full and floriferous, though it is forgiving of occasional neglect.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Unplugged So Blue Mealycup Sage (True-Blue Non-Stop-Blooming Salvia farinacea)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun; Unplugged So Blue is a true-blue mealycup sage selection that blooms continuously without deadheading.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun after frost danger has passed; this mealycup sage selection holds a true, saturated blue flower color rather than the more violet-blue tone of many farinacea cultivars. Unplugged So Blue blooms continuously from spring through frost without any deadheading, thriving in heat and humidity while tolerating drought once established. It attracts bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds steadily and resists deer browsing, performing equally well in containers and in-ground plantings. In zones 8-10 it may behave as a short-lived perennial, while further north it is grown as a warm-season annual.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Unplugged White Mealycup Sage (White-Flowered Non-Stop-Blooming Salvia farinacea)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun; Unplugged White bears white flowers with silvery calyxes densely packed on upright spikes, blooming continuously without deadheading.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part sun after frost danger has passed; this mealycup sage selection descends from a species native to Florida, Texas, and New Mexico, giving it strong heat and humidity tolerance. Unplugged White is self-cleaning, bearing white, two-lipped flowers with silvery calyxes densely packed on upright spikes from spring through frost without deadheading. It tolerates drought once established though it looks best with regular watering, and trimming back the upper third of the plant after a dry spell encourages fresh, full regrowth. It attracts bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds while resisting deer browsing.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
